newsitem.title: BELGIUM: France, Germany pledge to drive EU integration.
newsitem.headline: France, Germany pledge to drive EU integration.

text.p: France and Germany, pledging to remain the driving force behind European Union integration, said on Monday they were renewing efforts to stop lone EU countries from blocking others that want to pool national sovereignty.

At a joint news conference that immediately drew fire in the Netherlands, the new EU president, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and his French counterpart, Herve de Charette, said the two countries were committed to being Europe's engine.
"The French and Germans are closing ranks and we hope that our German-French tandem will be the stimulus for further integration," Kinkel said.
Kinkel and de Charette were speaking on the sidelines of the first meeting of EU foreign ministers this year, also the first under the Dutch presidency that begin on January 1.

They said a key element in Franco-German cooperation would be to push for a flexibility clause to be introduced into the EU treaty, currently under review in the inter-governmental conference (IGC), due to be completed in June.
The idea is to create a system to allow some countries to forge ahead of others. It is in part a response to reluctant integrationists such as Britain.
With the EU set to expand rapidly into eastern Europe over the next few years, most EU countries agree that some flexibility is needed. The crunch comes when negotiators try to define it.

Under a proposal put forward last year by Paris and Bonn, a broad clause would be introduced into the treaty, allowing groups of countries to move ahead. But a key element is that no single country would be allowed a veto on such a move.
"No member state must be able to block the other," Kinkel said.
This stance is vehemently opposed by Britain -- which favours allowing countries to move ahead, but only by the unanimous vote of all the EU states -- and has raised concerns in other capitals.
Sweden, Denmark and Portugal are also wary of moves to do away with unanimity, fearing the creation of an inner core of countries that would set rules without the others.
"Any decision must be agreed by all," David Davis, Britain's European affairs minister, said.
Italy on Monday also made public its view on flexibility -- or enhanced cooperation as it is sometimes known in EU-speak -- saying it should not be used to sideline countries.
"Enhanced cooperation should be the exception and not the rule, not used by a minority to forge ahead while the rest look on," it said in a statement.
Rome, however, is prepared to do away with unanimity.

De Charette and Kinkel, meanwhile, emphasised the continuing desire of the two countries to be the "motor" of European integration, noting that there had been some 100 bilateral meetings on Europe last year.
The news conference, however, was attacked in some quarters as being an attempt by the two large countries to wrest control of the political debate.
Some Dutch media painted the move as a "political coup" against the Netherlands by big states seeking to throw their weight around.
They reported that the Dutch liberal VVD party had already tabled a parliamentary question on the issue in The Hague.
